power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Currently, there are no specific suicide prevention programmes for primary (elementary) schools within the UK.
However, given the rise in suicidal thoughts and/or behaviours amongst children under 11 years, the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need for these programmes need to be assessed.
Aims: This qualitative scoping study aimed to explore whether there is a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools and, if so, what these should look like.
92 participants took part in the study.

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with mental health professionals (N= 22), school staff (N= 8), and parents of children who had experienced suicidal ideation, behaviours, or been bereaved by suicide (N=7).
Focus groups were conducted with secondary school students (N= 36) and primary school students (N= 19) across 5 schools.
Data were analysed using thematic framework analysis.

Results: Three main themes were identified: 1) the necessity of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, 2) barriers affecting delivery and potential solutions, 3) the transition period from primary to secondary school.

Overall, participants supported the need and acceptability of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, particularly due to the rising concerns about suicidality among younger children and evidence that suicide-related discussions are already occurring within peer groups.
However, careful consideration needs to be given to ensure it is delivered in a safe and ageappropriate way, with a focus on dispelling myths, promoting help seeking, and increasing knowledge.

Within the United Kingdom (UK), there are no explicit suicide prevention programmes for children in primary (elementary) schools (aged 4-11 years), despite rates of suicidal ideation, behaviours, and attempts increasing in children and young people (CYP) (1, 2).

text.text: However, despite increasing evidence that primary school-aged children may be experiencing or exposed to suicide ideation, attempts, or bereavement, they do not currently have routine access to suicide prevention education to reduce myths and stigma or provide information to promote help-seeking.

An increasing risk of suicidal ideation as children transition to secondary school suggests an upstream approach in primary schools may be beneficial, intervening early to equip CYP with help-seeking skills and prevent later suicidal behaviours/attempts.

However, there is currently limited information on suicide prevention initiatives in primary schools, including whether there is a perceived need for them, whether they would be acceptable to deliver and, if so, what they would need to look like.
Conversely, there is evidence to suggest that suicide prevention programmes can be implemented safely and effectively within secondary schools.
Schools are frequently viewed as a source of universal access for CYP, providing opportunity to incorporate early preventative programmes (27, 28).

text.text: However, a commonly cited concern regarding suicide prevention education is that discussing suicide may be distressing, developmentally inappropriate, or could inadvertently introduce suicidal ideas (32).

text.text: Limited information currently exists on the effects of discussing suicidality with CYP under 11, including whether it is safe or necessary.
Although young children face multiple risk factors, suicide prevention programmes have yet to be encouraged.
Hence, this study aimed to explore the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need of a suicide prevention programme in UK primary schools.

The scoping study specifically looked to explore (1) whether there is a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools and, if so, what these should look like, and (2) whether primary school children want mental health interventions and what they would like to learn about.
A qualitative design was utilised to explore the experiences of stakeholders across England.
Specifically, semi-structured, one-to-one interviews were conducted with school staff (SS), mental health professionals (MHP), and parents (P) who had supported children with suicidality.
Focus groups were conducted with primary school pupils (PSP) and secondary school pupils (SSP).

text.text: Adult stakeholders and schools were recruited through voluntary/opportunity sampling via adverts distributed by email to existing networks of the authors and on networking apps (e.g., LinkedIn).
Individuals interested in participating were provided with a participant information sheet and opt-in consent form.
Gatekeepers recruited students from Years 5-6 in primary schools (aged 9-11 years), and Years 9-11 in secondary schools (aged 13-16 years).
They were asked to select students of mixed ages, different sociodemographic backgrounds and experiences.
Gatekeepers were asked to exclude students experiencing mental health difficulties or suicidality, or for whom participation might be distressing.
Once students were selected by the school, verbal consent was taken from the students and parental information sheets and opt-in consent forms were sent out.
Only students with parental consent could participate.
Written assent was then taken from students at the beginning of the focus groups.
Students were also provided with an information sheet prior to assent, using 'childfriendly' language and read aloud by the research assistant.
Focus groups were conducted with 3-6 students per group (although one individual interview was conducted because no other parents/carers returned consent forms).
Thirty professionals participated (see Table 1).

text.text: Twenty-two were mental health professionals (including charity workers, therapists, researchers) and eight were school staff members.
Participants varied across age and gender, with the majority identifying as female (63%).
While the majority participated in interviews, two focus groups were conducted within an organisation at the participants' request; one included six participants and another three participants.
Seven parents of children who had experienced suicidal ideation or behaviours, or who had been bereaved by suicide took part in one-to-one semi-structured interviews (see Table 2).

text.text: The parental interview schedule was similar, exploring whether they felt a need for suicide prevention in primary schools, why, and what it should involve.
Secondary school students were asked about whether they thought it would be appropriate to have a suicide prevention programme in primary school and if so, what should or should not be included.

Focus groups with primary students did not mention suicide to ensure safety and instead focused on what participants knew about mental health, what they would like to learn about, and how they would like to be taught.
All interviews with adult participants were completed online and recorded via Microsoft Teams.
Interviews and focus groups with CYP were completed in their schools.

At the beginning of the focus group, the researcher emphasised to all participants that they could stop the study at any time point, skip questions, and did not have to talk about any individual experiences.

Participants were informed that there was no set suicide prevention programme that the researchers were trying to implement; this was highlighted so that participants felt comfortable to talk freely without feeling like there was a right or wrong answer.
All interviews and focus groups were conducted by the research assistant (BA).
Focus groups were conducted in a private, quiet room to ensure confidentiality.
After each session, participants received an age-appropriate support document signposting relevant services and were encouraged to ask questions.
Interviews and focus groups lasted on average 37 minutes (8-66 minutes).
Transcripts were reviewed and edited by the research assistant to ensure accuracy and anonymity.
Data were analysed using NVivo 15 using the five stages of thematic framework analysis (familiarisation, coding, creating themes, reviewing themes, and defining themes) (42).

text.text: The researcher (BA) first familiarised themselves with the data and generated initial codes, before engaging in discussions with other members of the research team (EA, PS) to generate initial themes.
Remaining transcripts were then coded against this framework, and themes were reviewed and defined.
Final themes were agreed, defined, and interpreted by the research team.

Mental health professionals and school staff discussed how suicidal thoughts and behaviours were 219 common in primary schools and described working with primary-aged children who had struggled with 220 suicidality: "I was experiencing children who were disclosing suicidal ideation or thoughts of suicide, 221 thoughts of ending their own life from around the age of seven, eight."
(MHP7).

They described 222 children experiencing passive suicide ideation, often referring to wanting to be dead or not wanting to 223 be here, rather than active ideation or plans: "She would regularly say that she didn't want to be here 224 anymore or 'wish I was dead,' you know, and at the age of like 9 and 10" (SS26).

text.text: For those whose difficulties started later, parents believed that prevention sessions earlier on in primary school could have helped their child before they reached a later crisis, equipping them with knowledge of how to seek help: "and I think back to when they were 9 or 10, if they'd been having, you know, sort of awareness sessions in school around suicide at that age, I think it definitely could have helped" (P1).

Many participants mentioned that primary-aged children were already aware of suicide, particularly because their peers were sharing suicidal thoughts with them, often before teachers were aware that there was a problem: "I wouldn't just be thinking about the children who experience those thoughts, but the children who are hearing from their peers that their peers experiencing that, because a lot of the time they hear it before we do" (SS8).

Both parents and professionals also mentioned that their primary-aged children have heard suicide being discussed by other children in school: The role of the Internet/media Professionals felt that CYP were spending more time on social media than previous generations, which they partly attributed to parental concerns about children's safety outside, with implications for social relationships and CYP's mental health: "I think another driver for that is social media, again, because I think as parents, we don't feel that it's safe for them to go out… It's sad because, you know, we're social animals we need that sort of human interaction, but their friendships are not as deep anymore because everything's digital, so they, you know, they don't hug each other or anything anymore.
It's sad."
(MHP4) Parents also described difficulties navigating the "online world", which was referred to as a "third parent" (P2), as well as having a "dehumanising effect" (P5).

Professionals highlighted how suicide, mental health, and self-harm are themes featured in many films and television series, which could be seen positively, by rising awareness, or negatively, by trivialising the topic.

They felt this meant children are aware of what suicide is and, in some cases, may increase the cognitive availability of suicide for vulnerable CYP: "Media portrayals, like certain TV series intend to raise awareness, but they can sometimes make suicide seem more common or less serious.
And in some vulnerable young people, it could even increase harm because some people do take things the wrong way."

(SS28) CYP emphasised how necessary it is that children are taught about online safety and the dangers of social media, to ensure they are equipped with the skills needed to keep themselves safe: "but if they didn't learn it [online safety] from their parents, they're going to learn it somewhere else.
They're not going to know what to do then."
(SSP4).
Professionals emphasised that by prohibiting CYP from accessing social media, they would do it without the parents' knowledge, promoting unsafe use: "I think that might be the risk.
Parents worry that if they're exposed to it [suicide], but a lot of the time these children are on social media and being exposed to so much anyway without parents overseeing it."

text.text: Secondary school students also suggested that students should be taught about identifying "truth and fake news" (SSP12).

The need for suicide prevention programmes was emphasised by professionals due to the lack of available mental health services, with some CYP needing more support than schools could provide but not meeting the high thresholds for CAMHS support: "CAMHS is exceptionally challenging for us to get in place, even when we know that that's what we need.
And then what we find is young people don't reach the criteria, this threshold for CAMHS, which seems to get higher and higher and higher every single time I make a referral.
But then we have something in my area, which is called [organisation name], which also kind of provide support for young people.
But then if there's real suicide ideation or action planning or whatnot, then they're deemed too high for that [organisation name].
So, we've got these children that fall in this middle area."

(SS8) Another issue raised was the lack of accessible and effective support for young neurodivergent individuals, given that they are at increased risk of both mental health difficulties and suicide: "My daughter is autistic and has ADHD.

And so, I think for that group of children and young people, mental health services are particularly awful… they're just not equipped to care for, in my opinion, children, young people who've got kind of additional needs over and above 6 sessions of CBT."

(P3) With neurodiversity, participants had mixed feelings on how to best support these individuals with sensitive sessions, with some suggesting that "when it's adapted for neurodivergent children" (MHP4) it will be useful for all students and that the programme should be "inclusive by nature" (SS29).
However, other participants believed sessions should differ for neurodivergent individuals as "they don't learn in the same way and don't always take on the same message" (SS25).
Mental health professionals suggested that some neurodivergent individuals may need to "have some separate teaching or some teaching revisited" (MHP7).

A common barrier highlighted to programme delivery was parental concerns, related to religious, cultural, personal beliefs, or "because they don't understand something or they fear it" (MHP10): "if you say we're running this suicide prevention thing at primary school, that's going to make the parents go 'my kids are not doing that'" (P4).

Participants described how parents' discomfort around the topic could lead them to refuse participation, as with other personal, health, or relationship education sessions: "We always get big letters home about 'In this session, we're going to talk about sexual health or whatever.
If you've got concerns' and there are parents that will always contact the school with, 'I don't really want my child listening to this'."

It was also noted that the subjective experiences of parents can carryover onto the child, which in that case creates a bigger barrier: "I think there might be some resistance from parents… I think sometimes parent anxiety feeds into child anxiety and then, you know, that might be an issue" (MHP14).
Another barrier was the comfortability of school staff in discussing suicidality, particularly given the lack of training and knowledge.
Professional participants questioned whether they are equipped to deliver a programme on suicidality: "'am I the right person to deliver this?'"
(MHP5).
Some participants also noted that "members of staff who've dealt with that [suicidality]" (SS27) may find this particularly difficult.
When discussing who should deliver a suicide prevention programme, opinions varied.
Some believed that schoolteachers were unsuited due to "very little support or supervision" (MHP7) available for staff after delivering PSHE sessions.
It was also highlighted that teachers "might have certain views or values" (MHP7) around suicide, potentially affecting delivery.

Students preferred an external professional delivering the potential programme, with a teacher present, believing this would benefit everyone and ensure the message was communicated appropriately: "Like I'd rather them sit back and listen with the kids then and have someone else talk because they'll have their own opinions and they might not express it properly to the children."
(SSP6).

This was also supported by primary-aged students, who expressed the importance of the . students' comfortability and how students will feel safe by having their teacher present: "Kind of both because the classroom teacher, they've been with them longer.
You get to feel more comfortable with the teacher, but with another person in, they might have different views that they can learn."
(PSP1).

However, some students believed that having the teacher deliver the session would be more effective as teachers tend to become a secure figure in a student's life, therefore students "won't mind telling them if something wrong" (SSP3).
All participants felt it was important for everyone to be fully informed.

Participants described how understanding why the programme was being delivered would help teachers feel more comfortable around delivery: "I think if teachers know the statistics and if teachers understand the research as to why we're doing it, I think they would do it" (MHP2).

Similarly, informing parents that suicide is a current issue affecting CYP may prevent barriers: "I think it's being open and transparent to the parents early doors and sending out as much information as you possibly can and really highlighting exactly why you're doing it" (MHP4).

Most participants suggested workshops for parents and school staff before programme implementation, alongside involving them in its delivery, to alleviate concerns: "Parents need to be brought on the journey.
They need to understand why things are being done, the way that it's going to be done, have the opportunity to be able to ask questions."

(MHP 5) Despite recognising the programme's importance, participants also emphasised that CYP should have the option to not participate: "Children who have got, you know, are struggling with mental health, they do definitely need an opt out" (MHP30).

Primary school students also emphasised they should "have the choice" (PSP1) but felt that it was important for students their age to have lessons on mental health: "Yeah, give them the option to like do it because if they feel comfortable doing it, then I think you should learn about it" (PSP13).

text.text: They also discussed how this can be seen as both positive and negative: "there's a lot more people for you to be friends with, but then there's also a lot more people for you to not be friends with and have arguments with."
(SSP5).

The increase in workload was another challenge during the transition phase, as well as the fact that school gets more serious: "I think there's like definitely more work in secondary school and they also in secondary school like tell you about more topics and they don't like shield you from anything."
(SSP2).

Ultimately, students described the transition as "just a stressful experience in itself" and "nervewrecking" (SSP5), highlighting its potential impact on emotional wellbeing, which could potentially lead to suicidal thoughts.
Besides the external changes, participants also highlighted that children experience puberty and hormonal changes, which can affect emotional wellbeing.
They therefore emphasised the importance of teaching children to regulate heightened emotions and access support: "You've got obviously then puberty may have come before, but maybe after.
So, you've got all that kind of emotional change as well and, you know, physical changes happening in the body and, you know, they can evoke real big emotions.
And I think that, you know, those big emotions need to be addressed."

(SS30) As a result, participants highlighted the importance of CYP knowing how to seek help and support peers, particularly in Year 6, to equip them before transitioning to secondary school: "we need to equip them with those skills and knowledge to have that awareness, but also how to support themselves or how to support a friend."

School staff also emphasised the value of preventative sessions, particularly around death in general and grief: "Talking about, you know, dying and the impact of real-life, impact of how life carries on for other people and on the point of view of other people who are left behind" (SS30).
Participants emphasised that the stigma surrounding suicide can hinder help-seeking and the ability to have open conversations.

Therefore, participants stressed the need for equipping CYP to develop emotional literacy to be able to support one another: "Even at the very lowest level, being able to be there for each other as friends, as kids together and being able to support one another through difficult times."

text.text: Although participants placed strong emphasis on the struggles CYP face when moving to secondary school, not all students are negatively impacted.

However, participants argued that all students should receive support and knowledge around mental health and suicide prevention, even if they do not need it at the time, as they might need it later, either for themselves or to support others: "they might not think it's that important, but I think when they get older, they'll realise how important it is to have the lesson" (PSP13).

Early prevention was also perceived to have the potential to reduce suicidality: "If we can get into that really early with people, then we're not going to have the numbers of suicides that we're having now in adults."
(MHP9).
Parents were also identified as a barrier to children accessing support by not allowing them to receive "useful information" (P3).
Participants linked this to suicide stigma and the contribution of generational attitudes, highlighting the importance of early preventative care to challenge these patterns.
This was supported by primary students discussing mental health: "when you are older and you have like kids of your own, they might need like help" (PSP13).
This scoping study investigated the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary school.

text.text: Participants therefore emphasised teaching about broader themes, including emotional literacy, help-seeking, coping skills, and identifying trusted adults, while ensuring that suicide-related content is introduced sensitively.

Parents and professionals highlighted that suicide had become a topic of playground conversation, with schools frequently responding to disclosures of suicidal thoughts to peers, despite the topic not having been formally discussed in school.
Furthermore, bereavement by suicide is becoming increasingly common (44), with professionals emphasising that there are many children who have been bereaved by, and exposed to, suicide (45).
text.formatted: Furthermore, bereavement by suicide is becoming increasingly common <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref>, with professionals emphasising that there are many children who have been bereaved by, and exposed to, suicide (45).

text.text: This suggests that children may already be accessing suicide-related information, often without adult oversight, increasing risk of misunderstanding and misinformation.
Developmentally appropriate prevention programmes could, therefore, provide a structured and supportive context for discussing these issues.
This finding supports evidence that children often disclose distressing thoughts to friends before seeking help from adults (46).
text.formatted: This finding supports evidence that children often disclose distressing thoughts to friends before seeking help from adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(46)</ref>.

text.text: A systematic review highlighted that 24% of studies showed that adolescents preferred informal support from friends and family rather than from health professionals (47), highlighting the importance of providing children with accurate information and signposting.

This was particularly emphasised in relation to social media and Internet use, with many children accessing the Internet without supervision and being exposed to inappropriate and harmful content, including suicide and self-harm (48).
text.formatted: This was particularly emphasised in relation to social media and Internet use, with many children accessing the Internet without supervision and being exposed to inappropriate and harmful content, including suicide and self-harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(48)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, one in four children aged eight have their own mobile phones in the UK, and 81% of girls aged 7-21 experience upsetting behaviours online, including suicide and self-harm content (49, 50), emphasising the need for online safety sessions.
text.formatted: Indeed, one in four children aged eight have their own mobile phones in the UK, and 81% of girls aged 7-21 experience upsetting behaviours online, including suicide and self-harm content <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">50)</ref>, emphasising the need for online safety sessions.

text.text: Additionally, during a focus group, a primary school student suggested that suicide should be a topic to be discussed within the potential programme.
While this shows that children are already aware of suicide, it also suggests an interest in learning more.
This was also apparent among secondary school students, as they stated that they had learned about suicide in primary school without anyone teaching them.
Primary school students expressed a further interest in mental health lessons, particularly because it was lacking in their current school.
Providing CYP with factual information is important, as over-simplifying topics of suicidality can result in misinterpretation, and potentially negative outcomes (51).
In particular, the transition from primary to secondary school was highlighted as a key issue affecting CYP, and where suicide prevention education may be beneficial.
This period often coincides with physical and hormonal changes (52), alongside changes in environment, routine, and academic responsibility (54, 55), which may affect emotional wellbeing (57).

text.text: Participants emphasised the value of accessible, school-based support (37, 38), including education for primary school students on selfhelp, advocating for themselves and others, and knowing how and where to seek help.

text.text: Although not all CYP experience mental health difficulties during the transition phase, participants felt it was still necessary to equip everyone with the knowledge and guidance on how to seek support and support others, for present or future use.
This is particularly relevant to suicide prevention, given that 20% of CYP had reported that in 2023, they had seriously considered suicide according to the Youth Risk Survey (56).
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant to suicide prevention, given that 20% of CYP had reported that in 2023, they had seriously considered suicide according to the Youth Risk Survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(56)</ref>.

text.text: However, not all participants felt that suicide prevention was appropriate in primary schools, and there were some concerns that it may be distressing.

With suicide being a sensitive topic, there is a lot that needs to be considered when developing a new programme, particularly regarding the comfort and safety of the students, and how it should be integrated.
Parental concerns were discussed in almost all interviews and focus groups, with the main concern being their lack of understanding of the topic and fear of the unknown.

Indeed, suicide is still a stigmatised issue, and it is this stigma that induces the increased rates of suicide and self-harm (57,58), particularly because of the lack of knowledge people have on the matter (59).

text.text: Whilst parental barriers were highlighted as a key issue, participants suggested that if parents were more included and informed on the subject, it would help them understanded the necessity of programme and feel more comfortable (60).

text.text: Staff comfort and confidence was another barrier, with limited training regarding suicide (61).

text.text: Teachers also reported a lack of support when delivering PSHE lessons, including no supervision or debriefing opportunities.

Participants had mixed opinions on whether a suicide prevention programme would be best taught by the classroom teacher or by a mental health professional due to the comfortability of the students and the knowledge of the teachers.

Although, extended literature shows that there is a precedent for external professionals delivering a sessions as well as providing training for school teachers (62, 63), so that they are able to support the students further.

text.text: Participants also emphasised that students should be able to choose whether to attend such sessions, highlighting the Overall, given the prevalence of suicidality among CYP, participants perceived a need for a suicide prevention programme in primary schools, delivered by teachers or external professionals, instead of CYP encountering suicide-related information informally through peers or online.
However, the development and possible implementation of a programme need to be carefully considered.

Given the sensitivity of the subject, participants suggested that it may be most appropriate for Year 6 students (10-11 years), with a focus on self-help, available resources and techniques, and signposting for themselves or others.
This could build upon lessons in earlier Years around emotional wellbeing and mental health.
Online safety, including appropriate Internet use and reporting concerns, and preparation for the transition to secondary school were also key topics that participants suggested.
However, participants emphasised that consent should be sought, and that the topic of suicide should be introduced sensitively, safely, and, in an age-appropriate way.
Although this current study explored the need for a suicide prevention programme in primary schools with a wide variety of stakeholders, some limitations should be considered.
All participating schools were from Northwest England, and only one primary school contributed, which may affect the transferability of the findings.

Whilst the current study had a large sample size with a variety of stakeholders, data on ethnicity and socioeconomical backgrounds as well as the gender of students was not collected, therefore it is recommended that full demographical information is collected from all participants in order to achieve representative data for future studies.

Overall, the findings suggest that primary school suicide prevention education is both needed and acceptable to key stakeholders, given growing concerns about suicidality among younger children and evidence that suicide-related discussions are already occurring within peer groups.

However, implementation should be approached cautiously and supported by clear guidance to ensure content is developmentally appropriate, evidence-based, and delivered safely within a robust safeguarding framework.

Future policy should look to support the integration of suicide prevention within wider . mental health education, alongside staff training, parental engagement, clear referral pathways, and a 507 focus on emotional literacy, help-seeking, and access to trusted sources of support.

The qualitative findings generally indicated a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools, although there was hesitancy for some.
Participants emphasised that many primary school-aged children experience suicidal ideation, and mental health professionals reported supporting CYP as young as seven years old.

This is consistent with national data indicating 109 suicide deaths among 10-to 17-year-olds in 2023 (3) and with Miller et al.'s (43) findings that almost half (45.92%) of children aged 5-10 years reported passive or active suicidal ideation.
Nevertheless, participants highlighted that children's awareness and understanding of suicide varies.
This suggests that caution is needed when implementing school-based suicide prevention programmes, as interventions may introduce some children to suicide for the first time.
